questions.q: What is an environment path, per this lesson?
options: A single sandbox used for every stage of testing
The sequence of orgs a change moves through in order before reaching production, with each stage designed to catch a different class of problem
A Salesforce report showing user login history
The physical data center location of an org
questions.explain: An environment path is a deliberate sequence of stages -- development, integration/QA, UAT, production -- each catching problems at a cheaper point than the next.

questions.q: Which sandbox type does this lesson describe as a complete copy of production data and metadata, suited to final UAT or performance testing?
options: Developer sandbox
Developer Pro sandbox
Full sandbox
Partial Copy sandbox
questions.explain: A Full sandbox is a complete copy of production -- all data, all metadata -- making it the right choice when a test needs to reflect production exactly, at the cost of a longer refresh cycle.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the refresh cycle of Partial Copy and Full sandboxes is a real planning constraint?
options: Because those sandboxes can never be refreshed at all
Because sandbox refresh is instantaneous and never needs planning
Because refresh cycles only matter for Developer sandboxes
Because if a team needs current production data and the sandbox was last refreshed weeks ago, that scheduling dependency has to be accounted for in advance, not discovered the week of release
questions.explain: Partial Copy and Full sandboxes refresh on multi-day or multi-week cycles, so a deployment plan has to account for whether the sandbox's current data is recent enough for the test at hand.

questions.q: What does a release calendar do, per this lesson?
options: It lays out scheduled internal releases alongside external, non-negotiable events like seasonal upgrade weekends and sandbox preview windows, giving every team visibility into what else is landing nearby
It only tracks Salesforce's own seasonal releases and ignores internal releases
It is a Salesforce Setup feature that auto-schedules deployments
It replaces the need for a go/no-go checkpoint
questions.explain: A release calendar combines internal release scheduling with external platform events so teams can see conflicts and plan change-freeze periods, rather than discovering overlaps after the fact.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a go/no-go checkpoint, as described in this lesson?
options: To let a deployment proceed automatically once it's scheduled, with no further review
To replace the Change Advisory Board entirely
To force a deliberate, conscious decision confirming every precondition (testing complete, rollback plan ready, right people available) is actually met before the deployment proceeds
To determine which sandbox type a team should use
questions.explain: The go/no-go checkpoint is an explicit, named decision point specifically so a deployment doesn't proceed by inertia just because it was already on the calendar -- someone has to actively confirm readiness.
